setting: a family-run bakery chain adding evening pizza service (Tamarind Hearth Bakers)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for our co‑owner Maria Alvarez about launching an evening pizza service at our three Tamarind Hearth Bakers locations. Currently we serve 320 customers per day on average, generating $45,000 in daily sales of breads and pastries. We plan to invest $52,000 in two deck‑oven rigs (each quoted $24,500) and allocate $8,000 for kitchen remodels, expecting pizza sales to add $5,200 per week at a $12 average ticket. I’m assuming 30 % of our existing daytime customers will stay for pizza and that a new evening crowd will contribute another 15 % of foot traffic. The biggest unknown is the actual demand on Friday‑Saturday nights, especially from non‑regulars. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this rollout could fail (including any cost or risk I might have missed), and tell me what specific result—such as weekly pizza revenue falling below $2,000 for two consecutive months—should trigger us to stop or re‑evaluate the plan. Please keep the answer focused for Maria, who will decide at the next board meeting on June 12.

setting: a regional freight broker building an in-house load-matching app (Quillfeather Logistics)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our COO, next Thursday (Oct 24). We’re planning to build an in‑house load‑matching app for Quillfeather Logistics with a projected rollout in 18 months and a total budget of $2.3 million. The business case assumes we can capture 120,000 loads per month at $0.85 per transaction, generating $120k monthly (120,000 × $0.85) and a 5 % month‑over‑month growth in volume. We’re budgeting $350k for the dev team, $200k for cloud infrastructure, and $150k per year for support – the latter isn’t reflected in the current cash‑flow model. The main assumption is that carriers will adopt the app within six months of launch, but we have no data on carrier churn after adoption, which is a real unknown. We’re comparing our cost structure to CarrierConnect, a SaaS provider that charges $1.00 per transaction, but we haven’t accounted for their integration fees or the fact that their platform already includes a $300k onboarding cost we’ll incur separately. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the primary ways this plan could fail, and specify the exact metric or event that would trigger us to kill the project or pivot. Thanks.

setting: a dental clinic group offering a monthly membership plan instead of insurance billing (Brightwater Dental)
prompt: I’m preparing a brief for Dr. Maya Patel, the owner of Brightwater Dental, and I need you to stress‑test the membership proposal before I present it at the June 30 board meeting. We plan to launch a $99 per month “Smile Club” on July 1 2025, targeting our existing 4,200 patients and an expected 12% new‑patient acquisition from local advertising (budget $150 per lead). Our model assumes that 30% of our current patients will convert, generating $5.0 M in annual revenue (we’ve calculated $99 × 12 months × 4,200 × 0.30 = $15.2 M, then applied a 67% discount for anticipated churn—see the spreadsheet). The pilot in 2022 showed a 12% churn rate, so we expect a similar figure. We’re not counting the extra cost of hiring two dental assistants (estimated $80 k each per year) or the potential impact of a pending state regulation that could limit direct‑to‑consumer dental plans—this is the real unknown. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three main ways this could fail, and specify the result (e.g., net‑margin falling below 8% after six months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the plan.

setting: a craft-glass studio moving from wholesale to direct online sales (Ashgrove Glassworks)
prompt: I’m drafting the pitch for Ashgrove Glassworks to move a $1.2 million annual wholesale operation (30 % gross margin, 800 pieces sold Q3‑2023) into a direct‑to‑consumer online channel. The plan is to launch an e‑commerce site in Q2 2025 with a $45k build budget, run a $150k digital‑marketing campaign, and target $250k in online sales the first year at a 20 % margin. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push forward, the main ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you see), and the specific result that would trigger us to kill or pivot the plan (e.g., a KPI threshold).

setting: a city bike-repair cooperative opening a second shop across town (Wheelhouse Collective)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal to take Wheelhouse Collective’s second location to Sam, our board member, and I need it stress‑tested before the June 15 meeting. We plan to lease a 1,200‑sq‑ft space on 5th Avenue for $3,200 per month starting July 1, and we expect to staff it with two full‑time mechanics at $3,200 each per month plus a part‑time admin at $1,800. Our financial model assumes the new shop will capture 20 % more members than our current storefront, giving us $12,500 in monthly revenue for the first six months, and we’ve budgeted $8,000 for an initial inventory of 40 refurbished bikes. The model does not include any marketing spend, assuming word‑of‑mouth will be sufficient. The biggest unknown is how the nearby competitor, CycleFix, will price its services after they announce a summer promotion next week. Please give me: (1) a single recommendation on whether to proceed, (2) the three most likely ways this rollout could fail, and (3) the specific result that would trigger us to halt or pivot the project (e.g., a net profit below a certain threshold). setting: an independent bookstore launching a paid reading-club subscription (Marlowe and Finch Books)

The unknown is the actual average shipping distance cost, because we haven’t nailed down the carrier rates for the mixed‑size parcels we’ll send. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead as outlined, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or demand risk you spot), and the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot—e.g., a specific shortfall in member count or profit margin. Also note any arithmetic slip or flawed comparison you see in the numbers I’ve given.

setting: a county veterinary practice adding a mobile large-animal van (Copperfield Veterinary)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for Dr. Maya Patel, the owner of Copperfield Veterinary, to add a mobile large‑animal van to our county practice. setting: a solar installer offering zero-down leasing financed from its own balance sheet (Sunhollow Energy)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the zero‑down leasing plan I’m taking to our CFO, Dana Lee, on Thursday, March 1 2025. Sunhollow Energy has $12 million in cash and wants to finance 250 residential solar systems over the next 12 months, each priced at $15,000. That gives us an expected gross revenue of $36 million (250 × $1,200 × 120 months), but I’m aware we’ve left out $2 million in projected installation labor and a $500 per‑system cost for inverter replacements after year 8. The plan also assumes a 5 % default rate, yet we haven’t priced any early‑termination penalties. The biggest unknown is whether the state subsidy of $0.08 /kWh, slated to expire in 2026, will be renewed. setting: a language school replacing in-person classes with a self-paced app (Larkspur Language Institute)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Maya Patel, our CEO, and need it stress‑tested before I present it. Larkspur Language Institute currently runs 12 in‑person sites serving 4,500 students, averaging 15 learners per class, pulling $2.1 million in revenue against $1.2 million in operating costs. We also need a $200 k marketing push to acquire users, which I didn’t include in the total cost. I need you to give me one clear recommendation, outline the main ways this rollout could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the project—specifically if net new revenue after 12 months falls short of $150 k.

setting: a small brewery adding a canned hard-seltzer line (Ironbridge Brewing)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the canned hard‑seltzer rollout we’ll pitch to Maya Ren, our co‑founder and CFO, next Tuesday. We plan to start production on 15 Nov 2025, run a 12‑month pilot, and sell 60 000 cases (12 oz each) at $3.50 wholesale. We estimate the line will cost $140 000 for equipment, $30 000 for a new canning line retrofit, and $15 000 for label design, so we say total upfront spend is $185 000. The assumption is that our current distribution margin of 30 % stays unchanged with the new product. We expect a break‑even at 45 000 cases, which we calculate as 185 000 ÷ (3.50 × 0.30). The unknown is the licensing fee for the proprietary flavor blend, which the supplier quoted as “around $8 000” but hasn’t confirmed. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the three biggest ways the plan could fail, and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to kill the project (e.g., missing sales target by X% after 6 months).

setting: a landscaping firm buying an electric mower fleet (Greenmantle Grounds)
prompt: I need a short briefing for our CFO, Maya Patel, on the proposal to replace 12 of our gas mowers with a new electric fleet from VoltTrim. The quoted price is $9,800 per mower, plus $1,200 per charging station; we need three stations, so total hardware cost is $136,800. We’re assuming electricity will stay at $0.12/kWh, giving us a per‑hour operating cost of $0.24 versus $4.50 for diesel. Over a typical 2,000‑hour year per mower, we project $480 in electricity versus $9,000 in fuel, a $8,520 annual saving per unit. That adds up to $102,240 saved each year across the fleet. The plan also claims a five‑year battery life, but we have no data on degradation after the third year. The only unknown is the cost and time to install the required 240 V power upgrades at each site; the vendor estimates “a few weeks” but no dollar figure. Please give Maya one clear recommendation (go ahead, delay, or drop), list the three biggest ways this could fail (e.g., hidden install cost, battery wear, unrealistic fuel cost assumption), and tell us what specific result—such as actual electricity use exceeding $0.20/kWh or battery replacement needed before year three—would trigger us to stop or change course.

setting: a charter school network centralising back-office payroll (Oakline Academies)

setting: a regional credit union launching a buy-now-pay-later product (Millbrook Credit Union)

setting: a furniture maker offering a lifetime repair guarantee (Juniper Joinery)
prompt: Maya, I’m preparing a brief for the upcoming board meeting on our “Premium Lifetime Repair Guarantee” rollout for Juniper Joinery. We’ve modeled a 3‑year pilot starting July 1 2024 in three regional markets (Seattle, Austin, and Boston). The projection is $1.2 million in additional revenue, based on an assumed 8% lift in sales of our Mid‑Century line, which sells $15 million annually. setting: a food-truck group opening a permanent commissary kitchen (Rustwheel Eats)
prompt: Hi AI, I’m drafting a proposal for Rustwheel Eats’s founder, Maya Patel, to get approval for converting our flagship food‑truck fleet into a permanent commissary kitchen. Here are the key points: we’ve secured a 4,800 sq ft loft on Main Street with a 5‑year lease at $28,000 per year, and we estimate the build‑out will cost $210,000 (including $45,000 for equipment, $30,000 for ventilation, and $35,000 for permits). Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the main ways this plan could fail, and tell me what specific metric or outcome would trigger us to kill the project. setting: a farm-supply store launching a same-day delivery fleet (Dunmore Farm Supply)

setting: a laundromat chain installing app-controlled machines in all branches (Suds and Co.)
prompt: I’m the VP of Operations at Suds and Co., and I need to brief our CEO, Maya Patel, on the app‑controlled machine rollout. We have 12 locations, and the pilot we started on 2023‑03‑01 at the downtown Boston branch showed a 15 % rise in usage, but we only tracked 40 % of the total machines because the other 60 % still ran manually. The budget we presented to the board assumes each smart washer costs $150,000 including installation, so we quoted a total spend of $1.5 M for all sites (I realize the arithmetic should be $1.8 M, but that’s the figure we’ve been using). We’re assuming an average of 2.5 loads per day per unit and that 80 % of customers will adopt the app within three months of launch on 2024‑10‑01. The unknown is the exact integration cost with the third‑party payment gateway and any licensing fees, which we haven’t been able to get a firm quote on yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways this could fail (including the cost slip and adoption assumption), and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to stop or pivot the project. The answer is for Maya Patel.

setting: a hardware wholesaler migrating its order system in one weekend (Boltwell Supply)
prompt: I’m preparing to take the weekend migration plan for our order‑processing platform to our COO, Maya Patel, and I need it stress‑tested first. We have 3,500 SKUs and process an average of 1,200 orders per day; peak load on Black Friday reached 2,800 orders in a single hour. The plan is to shut down the current Boltwell legacy system at 10 p.m. on Saturday, June 5, 2025, and bring the new cloud‑native solution online by 10 a.m. Sunday, giving us a 12‑hour window. We’ve budgeted $150,000 for the migration, which we say is 15 % of our IT spend, and we expect to save $200,000 per year on licensing, though we haven’t added the $75,000 one‑time integration fee that the vendor quoted. My stated assumption is that the new platform can handle twice today’s peak load without performance tuning. The real unknown is the cost of downtime for our top client, who could lose up to $10,000 per hour if orders aren’t processed. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the main ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to stop or change course.

setting: a cleaning-services company offering a guaranteed-satisfaction refund (Fernhill Cleaners)
prompt: Maya, could you stress‑test the “Premium Satisfaction Guarantee” rollout I’m about to pitch to our COO, Ravi Shah? We plan to launch it on 1 Oct 2025 across our three service zones (North, East, West). The idea is to charge a $49 monthly subscription that includes up to three deep‑clean visits per month, and if a client isn’t 100 % satisfied after the visit we’ll refund the entire month. We’ve modeled that with our current 12,000 households, a 15 % conversion will add $882,000 in revenue per year. We assume the refund rate will stay at the historical 2.8 % (based on our one‑off guarantee program) and that operating costs will rise by only 4 % (mainly extra labor at $13.50 / hr). The unknown is how competitors will react—if they introduce a similar guarantee within 60 days, we could lose up to 5 % of the projected sign‑ups. I need one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific metric (e.g., refund cost exceeding 4 % of subscription revenue for two consecutive quarters) that would trigger us to halt or pivot the program. Thanks.

setting: a regional newspaper putting its archive behind a paywall (Alderton Courier)
prompt: Maya, our Chief Revenue Officer, will be the one I’m briefing on Friday, so I need a concise brief to stress‑test the paywall proposal for the Alderton Courier archive. We have about 120,000 monthly unique readers as of June 2024, and I’m assuming 15% of them will convert to paid subscribers once we lock the archive behind a $12 monthly fee. That gives us roughly 20,000 paying users and, on paper, $240,000 per month or $2.9 million a year. We expect ad revenue to fall by 20% (from $1.5 million to $1.2 million) after launch, and we’ll need $500k for the initial technical rollout plus $250k for digitizing the 1950‑1975 microfilm collection. Our team of three developers will handle integration, but we haven’t priced any legal compliance work for GDPR and CCPA, nor have we factored the likely churn after the first three months (we have no data on that). I’d like you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the main ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., if month‑one revenue falls below $100k) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the initiative.

setting: a private tutoring marketplace cutting its commission from 20% to 12% (Candlewick Tutors)
prompt: Hi, I need you to stress‑test a proposal I’m taking to our COO, Maya Patel, tomorrow. Candlewick Tutors, our private tutoring marketplace, currently charges a 20% commission on each session. We plan to reduce that to 12% starting July 1 2024 to boost tutor acquisition. Our data shows we have 3,200 active tutors, an average session price of $75, and monthly GMV of $1.8 million. We estimate the lower commission will raise tutor sign‑ups by 15% and increase completed sessions by 8% within three months, offsetting the 8% drop in per‑session margin. The assumption is that the price elasticity for tutors is similar to that of students, which we haven’t measured. The unknown is how much our support and dispute‑resolution costs will rise with more tutors; we haven’t modeled that. Also, we overlooked a $120 k annual contract renewal fee for our payment processor that scales with transaction volume—if volume spikes, that fee could double. I need one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the biggest ways this could backfire, and the specific result (e.g., a net‑margin dip below 12% for two consecutive quarters) that would trigger us to halt the rollout.

setting: a plant nursery adding a houseplant-of-the-month club (Mossgate Nursery)
prompt: I’m drafting a brief for Jenna Torres, our CEO, about launching a “Houseplant‑of‑the‑Month” club at Mossgate Nursery. I need you to stress‑test the plan before I present it. The idea is to charge a $45 monthly fee, starting June 15 2025, and reach 200 members by the end of Q3. We have a 1,200 sq ft greenhouse that can hold the extra inventory, and we’ll allocate $8,000 for a targeted Facebook/Instagram campaign. I’m assuming 30 % of our existing 5,000 customers will sign up, which would give us about 1,500 members, but I’m scaling the pilot to 200 to keep risk low. The projection says 15 % churn after six months, giving us roughly $9,000 in revenue in the first quarter and a $1,000 profit margin after the $8,000 ad spend. The unknown is the per‑box packaging and shipping cost, which we haven’t priced yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or arithmetic issue you spot), and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us halt the program (e.g., if a specific metric falls short). Thanks.

setting: a climbing-gym operator opening a second, larger location (Cragside Climbing)
prompt: Maya, I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our founder, for the Cragside Climbing second location. We plan to lease a 12,000 sq ft warehouse on Oakridge Road, starting a 10‑month build‑out that should finish by 15 June 2025. The total capital budget is $2.1 M, of which $800 k is a bank loan at 5.5 % fixed. We’re assuming rent will be $15 per sq ft per month—the same rate we pay at the current 5,000 sq ft spot—but the landlord quoted $16.5 per sq ft in the lease draft. Our financial model projects 250 members now, growing to 350 by month 6 and 500 by month 12, based on a 30 % higher capacity and a 20 % increase in annual membership fees from $480 to $576. The model also assumes a 5 % churn rate and that we’ll break even after 18 months. The unknown is the city’s permitting timeline for the new climbing walls; the city has not given us a definitive date, and any delay past September 2024 would push opening to Q4 2025. Please give me one recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this plan could fail, and specify the result (e.g., a delay beyond September 2024 or a rent increase above $16 sq ft) that would trigger us to kill or rethink the project.

setting: a children's clothing brand switching to made-to-order production (Pebblestitch Kids)
prompt: Hi AI, I need to run my made‑to‑order (MTO) proposal past you before I present it to our COO, Maya Patel, next Thursday (Oct 24). Pebblestitch Kids currently holds $1.2 million in inventory, with an average lead time of 14 days and a turnover of 3.6 cycles per year. We forecast 120 k units for FY 2025 and expect MTO to cut warehousing by $250 k annually after an upfront tooling spend of $500 k. We’ve assumed our primary fabric supplier can increase capacity linearly from 80 k to 150 k yards per month without extra cost. The model says we’ll break even in 24 months, but we haven’t priced the extra $3 per unit shipping surcharge that would apply to 30 % of orders that fall outside the 7‑day promise we’ll give customers. The unknown we can’t estimate is the change in brand perception – will parents tolerate the wait or will churn rise? I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this plan could fail, and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to stop or pivot (e.g., if order fill rate drops below X% or cost per unit exceeds Y). Thanks.

setting: a rural clinic network adopting a shared electronic records vendor (Valleyview Health)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the plan I’m taking to our COO, Mara Patel, about moving PrairieCare Clinics to Valleyview Health’s shared electronic records platform. We run 12 rural clinics with 45 providers total. The vendor quote is $3.2 million for a three‑year license, plus $150,000 per clinic for on‑site hardware and $5,000 a month for support. We estimate we’ll save $120,000 a year in paper‑record handling and billing errors once the system is live. The rollout is scheduled for 18 months, starting 1 Oct 2026, with training in two‑week blocks at each site. My core assumption is that every clinic already has reliable broadband of at least 10 Mbps. The unknown is the integration cost with our existing lab interface, which the vendor hasn’t priced. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the main ways this could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed condition that would make us stop or change course (e.g., usage, cost overrun, timeline). Note that the $120k annual saving claim seems to ignore the $150k hardware per clinic, so look for that slip or any other hidden risk.

setting: a municipal water utility offering smart-meter leak alerts (Riverbend Water Authority)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal to take to our Chief Operations Officer, Maya Patel, and I need it stress‑tested before the board meeting on 15 Oct 2026. Riverbend Water Authority plans to retrofit 120,000 residential meters with smart‑leak sensors starting 1 Jan 2027, at a projected capital outlay of $2.5 million plus $300 k per year for data‑service fees. Our model assumes a 5 % adoption of the premium alert package, which we estimate will cut water loss by 8 % (about 1.2 million gallons per month) and generate $1.4 million in avoided treatment costs annually. The only unknown is the false‑positive alert rate; the vendor only gives a range of 2‑6 % from pilot data, and we have no firm figure for how many service calls that will trigger. One assumption we haven’t examined is that the 8 % reduction will hold across all districts despite varying pipe ages; we also omitted the extra labor cost of field crews responding to alerts, which could be $150 k per year. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the main ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed condition (e.g., if false‑positive alerts exceed X % or ROI falls below 3 %) that would cause us to kill or pivot the project.

setting: a recruiting agency charging candidates a placement fee (Northgate Staffing)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the pricing shift I’m about to pitch to our COO, Maya Patel. We currently place 45 candidates per month and charge a $12,000 placement fee per successful hire. I’m proposing we move to a revenue‑share model: 18% of the candidate’s first‑year salary, which we estimate will average $85,000, giving us about $15,300 per placement. I’m assuming 90% of our clients will accept the new terms because it aligns their cash‑flow with outcomes. The model would add a $1,200 onboarding cost per candidate (currently absorbed) to cover background‑check automation, and we’d need to increase our marketing spend by $8,000 per month to generate the same pipeline. We expect annual revenue to rise from $6.48 M to $7.0 M, a 7.9% increase, but I’m not sure how competitors will react—some charge a flat $10,000 fee and could undercut us. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go forward, list the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or arithmetic error you spot), and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to kill the plan (e.g., revenue drop below a threshold or churn above a certain %). The answer is for Maya.

setting: a coffee roaster launching a wholesale subscription for offices (Emberbean Roasters)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the wholesale office subscription we’re pitching to Maya Patel, our COO, before the board sees it next Tuesday, 2024‑11‑12. The plan is to launch on 2024‑11‑01 with a three‑tier offering: Basic at $120 per office per month (includes 10 12‑oz bags), Premium at $210 (20 bags + custom branding), and Enterprise at $350 (40 bags + weekly deliveries). We’re targeting 300 offices in the first quarter, assuming a 5% monthly churn and that 30% will upgrade to Premium after three months. We’ve modeled a gross margin of 65% based on a $45 per bag cost, but we didn’t include $8 per bag for shipping and handling. Our projections say we’ll hit $1.08 M in ARR by the end of Q1, but I may have added the Premium and Enterprise revenues together incorrectly. The big unknown is actual demand: we have only informal interest from 45 offices and no signed contracts. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this could fail (including any hidden assumptions), and tell me the specific metric or event that would trigger us to kill the program or pivot. Thanks.

setting: a regional theatre company selling a season pass priced below single tickets (Lanternlight Theatre)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal to present to Maya Patel, our board chair, on rolling out a new Lanternlight Theatre season‑pass program. The pass would be $120 for the full 2027 season (Jan 1–Dec 31), versus the current $50 average price for a single‑ticket purchase. Our goal is 5,000 passes, which we estimate will generate $600,000 in revenue; we’ve calculated the break‑even point at 3,200 passes because each show costs $8,000 to produce and we expect an average patron to attend 3 shows, generating $360,000 in ticket revenue (3 × $120 × 5,000 = $1.8 M, minus production costs). We’re budgeting $150,000 for a targeted digital‑marketing campaign and assuming a 10% conversion from our email list of 50,000 contacts. The key unknown is the uplift in ancillary sales (concessions, merch) from pass holders, which we haven’t quantified. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the program (e.g., if net profit after the first three months is negative). Also watch for any hidden cost or flawed assumption in my numbers.

setting: a marine-supply chain stocking drone-delivery for remote harbours (Anchorpoint Marine)
prompt: I’m putting together a pilot for Anchorpoint Marine to ship spare parts and safety kits to three remote harbours—Port Linton, Baycrest, and Harbor 7—using a fleet of delivery drones. The plan calls for 8 drones, each priced at $250,000, plus a $800,000 software integration fee, for a total budget of $2.8 M. We would start the test on 1 June 2025 and run it for 12 months, aiming to cut our last‑mile freight cost by $350,000 per year and reduce road‑fuel consumption by roughly 10,000 gallons. The assumption is that weather will allow at least 80 % of planned flight days and each drone can carry 150 kg per sortie. We expect maintenance to be $15,000 per month per drone, but we have not priced insurance or the potential customs clearance delays for the battery packs—that’s a real unknown. I need a short brief for our COO, Maya Patel: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways the pilot could fail, and the specific result (e.g., if monthly operating cost exceeds $250,000 after three months) that would trigger us to stop or re‑evaluate the whole idea.
